newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Tight security for Bougainville peace talks in NZ.
newsitem.headline: Tight security for Bougainville peace talks in NZ.

text.p: Tight security will surround leaders from Papua New Guinea's Bougainville Island when they arrive in New Zealand this weekend for talks aimed at ending a nine-year civil war, the army said on Friday.

Up to 60 rebel leaders, local officials and Papua New Guinea MPs representing Bougainville are expected to arrive in the South Island city of Christchurch on a New Zealand Air Force passenger aircraft early on Saturday.
The delegates will be accommodated at the nearby Burnham army camp for their talks, which are set to start on Monday and could last a week or more.

"We've increased security around the camp," captain Nigel Orr of the New Zealand Army told Reuters. He said about 1,000 soldiers were stationed at the base and an extra 30 military police and army personnel had been brought in.

Thousands of people have died in the Bougainville conflict since a landowners revolt began nine years ago. Up to 40,000 people have been displaced by the fighting and several rounds of internationally backed talks have failed to find a solution.
New Zealand's government revealed on Wednesday that it had set up and would fund the peace talks. It sent air force planes to PNG and the Solomon Islands on Friday to collect participants.
Wellington has insisted it will play no part in the discussions other than to facilitate a neutral location.
"We'll give them a comfortable environment and keep them happy and fed so they can get on with their peace talks," Orr said on Friday.
Warm clothes would be provided on arrival for the Bougainvilleans, who will come from the balmy tropics into the depths of a bitterly cold South Island winter.
Snow has been forecast around Christchurch on Friday with fine, if bracing, weather due to follow on Saturday.
The preliminary talks are expected to look at setting up a neutral zone on the Papua New Guinean island, policed by neutral peacekeeping forces, diplomatic sources say.
Foreign Minister Don McKinnon, who has called the discussions a first step, said the intention would be to bring the PNG government into the forum after this round is completed.

The Solomon Islands, Bougainville's neighbour, tried last month to broker peace talks between the unofficial Bougainville interim government, its associated paramilitary arm, the Bougainville Republican Army (BRA), and the PNG-backed Bougainville Transitional government.
But the government side did not show up.

The war on the copper-rich island also sparked PNG's most serious political crisis since independence when Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan earlier this year hired the Anglo-South African mercenary company Sandline to quell the Bougainville rebellion.
The move was strongly opposed by the PNG army and Sir Julius was forced to step down temporarily, eventually losing his seat.
He is set to remain in power until final election results are known on July 15.
